Journey doc corroborates in his own words (line 488): "decomposing the existing monolith into microservices by defining the boundaries", and the doc calls it "your *first* monolith-to-microservices decomposition, which makes it load-bearing for every architect interview."

Deque (résumé): "Championed decomposition of a monolith into **10–15 services**, splitting on independent scaling and database ownership rather than on team boundaries". Journey doc line 600 gives the rule verbatim: "a component became a microservice if it needed to scale independently or needed its own database. Each service owned its database; each database was multi-tenant."

The stronger-than-decomposition claim, journey doc line 198: "This was not one monolith split into pieces. Authentication was its own service in Java and Spring Boot, serving every product in the portfolio… Billing and subscription was a second cross-product service… Global configuration was a third. Ten to fifteen services by the time I left." The doc's own note (line 572): "the services you built were *cross-product platform services*, not just a decomposition of one application. A billing service consumed by every product in the portfolio is a materially stronger claim than 'we split the monolith.'"

SOLUTION ARCHITECTURE / DESIGN TRADE-OFFS — the JD asks for "Strong expertise in System Design and Solution Architecture". Journey doc line 597 records an evaluated trade-off with a chosen option and a reason: "Two options were evaluated: one database per customer, or a tenant/organisation-ID column on every table… Chosen: **organisation ID on every table**, with the tenant resolved from the **JWT** on every incoming request, so a single codebase served both models — no forked microservice versions." Plus the distinction that makes it architecture rather than plumbing (line 190): "The banks that would not share infrastructure kept their own database — against that same code. That is a deployment difference, not a second codebase, and holding that line is what kept it maintainable."

DISTRIBUTED SYSTEMS / SCALABILITY PATTERNS — the JD's "Design systems handling high traffic, high concurrency, large-scale workloads". Journey doc line 649: "a single message will result in 50 external calls", corroborated by code not memory (line 651): "`GROUNDING.md` counts roughly **48–58 external calls per message, of which 13–23 are OpenSearch calls**… The 50 figure is accurate and if anything conservative." Résumé: "Stewarded a **zero-downtime** upgrade from **PostgreSQL 9.6** to **Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL 13.x** across every axe Auditor instance".

scores.verdict:
9/10 — this is his strongest criterion, and it is the one the JD weights heaviest. Do not discount it.

The JD's Naukri skill tags are literally "System Design, Distribution System, Java, High Level Design, System Architecture", and its core ask is "Design and oversee architecture for scalable, distributed, microservices-based systems". Against that, he brings three monolith decompositions across three employers, two in Java and Spring Boot, plus the thing that separates an architect from an engineer who split a monolith: a stated, defensible boundary rule — "it earns its own process if it needs to scale independently or needs to own its data" — and cross-product platform services (auth, billing/subscription, global config) consumed by every product in a portfolio. That is a stronger microservices claim than the JD asks for.

Solution architecture is evidenced the way a panel actually tests it — as an evaluated trade-off with a chosen option and a reason. DB-per-customer versus org-ID-on-every-table, chosen deliberately, tenant resolved from the JWT, one code path, and the banks that refused shared infrastructure kept their own database against that same code because "that is a deployment difference, not a second codebase". Distributed systems is evidenced by a fan-out problem stated in nine words and corroborated by code rather than memory (48–58 external calls per message), a Go rewrite, a two-stream Kinesis design built explicitly for spike headroom, and an event-sourced DynamoDB single-table with CQRS and a deterministic snapshot exporter. Caching, async, messaging and event-driven — one full JD sub-block — is covered three times over across three eras, including a deliberate decision NOT to add Redis to a query path, which is the kind of answer that wins design rounds. Resiliency is not hand-waved: circuit breakers with a stated budget ("circuit breaker at 1.5s — defer panel · never block warm path"), per-tenant and per-role rate limits, idempotent resumable backfills, all in shipped code.

Two JD required sub-lines are only partly met — high availability designed against failure, and load balancing. Both are absent from the written record rather than contradicted by it, and one of them (load balancing) is almost certainly a documentation gap in the journey doc rather than a real one. The concurrency headline is a burst test and the two-stream design was never load-tested, both by his own admission. Those cost the tenth point. They do not cost more than that, because 19 years of "I get handed systems that work but can no longer scale the way they are built" is exactly the sentence this seat is buying, and because his zero-downtime record across ~300 instances is a harder availability skill than most candidates who can quote a nines figure actually possess.

Smallest honest lift for this criterion — all Rule 7 re-vectoring of real work, no new claims:
- Lead the VoltusWave block with the fan-out number, not the Kinesis shard count. "A single patient message fanned out into ~50 downstream calls" is the sentence that makes every follow-up write itself, and it is corroborated in code.
- Re-vector the Deque block to foreground the 10–15 services and the boundary rule ahead of the tenancy mechanics — the JD asks for microservices architecture first and multi-tenancy not at all.

Caching, asynchronous processing, messaging and event-driven architecture — four of the ten things this criterion names, and the whole of JD line 45 — are where he is close to a 10, on production evidence rather than reading. Amazon Kinesis in production with Enhanced Fan-Out and a 4→1,200 shard envelope is confirmed and not in dispute. A second async path (SQS → Lambda → S3) served the same product.
